reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents as acute, prolonged, spontaneous vertigo lasting days, with nausea, vomiting, and gait imbalance but without hearing loss
When hearing is also affected the term labyrinthitis is used, implying inflammation of the whole labyrinth rather than the vestibular nerve alone
The spontaneous nystagmus is horizontal-torsional, beats away from the affected ear, and is suppressed by visual fixation, consistent with a peripheral lesion
The head impulse test shows a corrective saccade toward the affected side, indicating a peripheral vestibular deficit
The HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus direction, test of skew) is more sensitive than early MRI for distinguishing peripheral neuritis from a posterior circulation stroke
Central features such as direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, or a normal head impulse test in an acutely vertiginous patient should raise concern for stroke
Management centres on short-term symptom relief and early vestibular rehabilitation to promote central compensation, avoiding prolonged vestibular suppressants
A thought to be post-viral or inflammatory process, it usually follows a monophasic course with gradual recovery
reference.pathophysiology: Vestibular neuritis is attributed to inflammation of the vestibular nerve, possibly from reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus in the vestibular ganglion, causing acute unilateral loss of peripheral vestibular input. The superior vestibular division is most often affected. The sudden asymmetry between the two vestibular systems generates a strong sense of rotational vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus. Over subsequent days to weeks, central adaptive mechanisms recalibrate the vestibular imbalance (central compensation), which underlies clinical recovery even if peripheral function does not fully return.
additionalDifferentials: Posterior circulation ischaemic stroke (cerebellar or brainstem)
Multiple sclerosis affecting brainstem vestibular pathways
additionalInvestigations: Bedside HINTS examination in acute continuous vertigo to separate peripheral from central causes
MRI with attention to the posterior fossa when central features or vascular risk are present
Audiometry to detect associated hearing loss suggesting labyrinthitis or other cause
Caloric testing or video head impulse testing to quantify vestibular function
Assessment of vascular risk factors when stroke is a consideration
redFlags: Central signs (direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, normal head impulse test) suggesting stroke rather than neuritis
Acute vertigo with other focal neurological deficits such as dysarthria, limb ataxia, or weakness
New severe headache or neck pain raising concern for vertebral artery dissection
Sudden hearing loss accompanying vertigo, which may indicate a vascular or other serious cause
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover over days to weeks as central compensation develops, though some have persistent unsteadiness or motion sensitivity; early vestibular rehabilitation improves recovery and reduces chronic dizziness.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing a cerebellar stroke as vestibular neuritis by relying on imaging that can be falsely reassuring early
Prescribing prolonged vestibular suppressants, which impair central compensation
Assuming any acute vertigo is peripheral without performing the HINTS examination
Overlooking associated hearing loss that changes the differential
Delaying vestibular rehabilitation and prolonging disability
management: Short-term vestibular sedatives and antiemetics such as antihistamines and prochlorperazine for severe acute vertigo and vomiting, discontinued early to avoid delaying central compensation
A short tapering course of corticosteroids in the acute phase, which may improve recovery of peripheral vestibular function
Early vestibular rehabilitation exercises to promote central compensation and reduce chronic unsteadiness
Rehydration and antiemetic support for patients unable to tolerate oral intake
Exclude posterior circulation stroke using the HINTS examination and arrange MRI when central features or vascular risk are present
Address vascular risk factors and arrange neurology or neuro-otology review for incomplete recovery or diagnostic doubt
